Tasty Blue, developed and published by Dingo Games, takes a concept so simple it borders on ridiculous—an ordinary goldfish that won’t stop eating—and transforms it into a surprisingly engaging and gleefully destructive arcade adventure. The premise wastes no time establishing its absurdity: a neglected pet escapes its tiny bowl and immediately begins devouring anything smaller than itself. From that moment forward, the game becomes a steady escalation of size, appetite, and chaos, gradually pushing the player from domestic aquariums into the open ocean, populated beaches, sprawling coastal cities, and eventually places no aquatic animal should realistically be. It plays like a children’s picture book that slowly mutates into a lighthearted disaster movie, yet maintains a cheerful, nonthreatening tone throughout. That tonal consistency is important—while destruction and consumption define the gameplay, everything is framed as slapstick comedy rather than violence.

The core mechanics revolve entirely around movement and consumption, yet the execution gives the game more longevity than expected. The player swims through two-dimensional levels, steering toward fish, crustaceans, debris, and unsuspecting humans, each bite contributing to growth. As the goldfish increases in size, the hierarchy of dangers gradually reverses—predators that once threatened the tiny creature eventually become snacks, and once-impassable barriers crumble under immense mass. This sense of continuous progression is the game’s engine, and Dingo Games has carefully structured levels to highlight the satisfaction of crossing those invisible thresholds, whether it’s the moment you finally eat a scuba diver or the first time you consume a boat. Even without complex controls, each stage feels like a miniature puzzle, asking players to find the safest, fastest, or most efficient route through the edible ecosystem.

To prevent the formula from becoming too predictable, the game introduces additional playable characters whose perspectives reshape familiar mechanics. The dolphin’s narrative, framed around intelligence and rebellion, introduces faster, sharper movement, while the shark’s campaign leans into brute force and unstoppable hunger. Though the gameplay remains largely unchanged, the change in physics, personality, and environmental design keeps the experience from stagnating. Levels gradually evolve in structure, incorporating timed escapes, maze-like layouts, hazards such as mines or harpoons, and escalating human responses ranging from panicked swimmers to military intervention. The humor intensifies as the player gets larger—seeing scientists, sailors, or submarines desperately attempt to stop an impossibly huge fish never loses its absurd charm.

Visual presentation plays a significant role in maintaining that charm. The art style is clean, colorful, and intentionally exaggerated, striking a balance between cartoon whimsy and environmental clarity. Characters have expressive panic animations, background details reinforce storytelling without slowing gameplay, and the overall aesthetic remains family-friendly even as the scale of destruction increases. Sound design enhances the absurdity—each gulp, crunch, and splash is exaggerated like a comedic sound effect, and the upbeat soundtrack reinforces the sense that nothing happening on-screen should be taken seriously. Tasty Blue is not trying to immerse players in realism; it’s inviting them into a sandbox of escalating silliness where the impossible becomes routine.

The game’s simplicity is both its design philosophy and its primary limitation. Because the mechanics remain consistent across campaigns, extended play sessions may begin to feel repetitive for players seeking strategic depth or mechanical evolution. There are no complex upgrade trees, branching storylines, or major systems layered on top of the core experience. Instead, replay value comes from perfecting levels, attempting to move efficiently, and enjoying the spectacle of unchecked growth. For some, especially younger players or fans of bite-sized arcade titles, this straightforwardness will feel refreshing. For others, it may limit the game’s staying power. However, the developers clearly understood their intended audience—those who want immediate, uncomplicated fun—and built the game with that clarity in mind.

What sets Tasty Blue apart from other casual growth-based games is its genuine sense of momentum. The escalation never feels abrupt or unearned; rather, players experience a continuous chain of small triumphs that lead to increasingly ridiculous outcomes. There is joy in simply moving through the world, testing boundaries, and discovering what new creature or construct will become edible next. The game encourages curiosity more than competition, chaos more than mastery, and delight more than dominance. It’s a rare example of a game that embraces absurdity without relying on shock value or cheap humor—its comedy emerges naturally from gameplay consequences rather than scripted jokes.

Tasty Blue succeeds because it understands exactly what it wants to be: a lighthearted, accessible, visually amusing power fantasy built around one core loop that always feels satisfying. It doesn’t ask players to invest emotionally, analyze systems, or commit to long sessions. Instead, it offers carefree entertainment—easy to start, hard to stop, and consistently amusing from beginning to end. Players of all ages can appreciate its charm, making it a great shared experience for families, casual gaming groups, or anyone who needs a joyful break from heavier or more demanding titles.

Ultimately, Tasty Blue is not memorable because of narrative depth, mechanical complexity, or technical innovation. It resonates because it captures the simple delight of play—of growing, exploring, and causing harmless mayhem in a world designed to support imagination rather than realism. It’s a reminder that games can still be funny, weird, and charming without overthinking themselves, and that sometimes all you need is a hungry goldfish and a world foolish enough to feed it.

Maybe an unpopular opinion, but this is a step-up from the original Tasty Planet. With more interesting environments and more forgiving gameplay, it just got me way more engaged and left me always curious to see what awaited me in the next level.

The most important thing in a game is obviously GAMEplay, so let's talk briefly about it. The most important thing: no more instakill enemies. One of the MOST frustrating experiences I had in Tasty Planet was sprinting towards an object that looked almost identically big to another object I had just eaten, then getting killed five minutes into the level and having to start from zero. I know, there's an outline and an arrow that points to the biggest thing you can eat, but considering the grey goo moves faster than a mouse on cocaine, it really didn't feel like it was my fault. And you can't stop to inspect objects for too long in Normal mode, because of the very strict time limit...

Which takes me to my next point: Tasty Blue finally removed the god-forsaken time limit. Now sure, Tasty Planet had a casual mode you could play, but you didn't get any medals for it. In Tasty Blue, you can take as long as you want, with the amount of stars you get (ranging from zero to 3) depending on how fast you beat the level.

About aesthetics: Tasty Blue absolutely has my favorite art style from the whole saga (admittedly, I haven't PLAYED Back for Seconds and Forever, but I've seen pictures). First of all, the sideways view provides much more interesting environments and the option for having different "layers" - instead of the same type of object being across the whole level like in Tasty Planet, you have planes and birds in the sky, kayaks and canoes on the water, small fish near the surface, sea stars and sea shells on the shore, whales and krakens in the depths... it just makes for a way more rich and lifelike world. 

Additionally, the background just looks way cooler, instead of the Tasty Planet style of just having a single texture spread across the entire map, only populated by eatable objects. And honestly, just think about it - the side view makes a lot more sense for a sea theme. The proof of this are the sea levels in Tasty Planet. Visually, they looked extremely bland, which I suppose is one of the reasons the sea stage only lasted three levels in that game.

Tasty Blue also has overall better effects. The water looks quite good, and so does the carnage setting.

Another major step-up introduced in Tasty Blue is the zooming out. Where in Tasty Planet the playable area always remained the same size as the grey goo got bigger, in most levels of Tasty Blue the screen will zoom out when the player reaches a certain size, introducing larger animals/objects and the smaller ones eventually fading out of view. This contributes to the layers effect I mentioned earlier, as well as introducing larger threats later into the level, rather than having to avoid huge, dangerous enemies right off the bad. Also, it gives you that satisfying feeling of growing bigger and "leveling up", which is really important in a game like this.

I found that the levels were quite more interesting than Tasty Planet's. While Tasty Planet was "a lot of the same" so to speak, occasionally interspersed with a "eat X amount of this or that" level, Tasty Blue had a lot more of "gimmick" levels that kept the gameplay fresh. The final level of each playable character (the "Tale of a ---") levels are the most fun; they are basically a "recap" of the character's story, starting with the environments from the first level and growing all the way to their biggest size.

Being fair, this is not to say that Tasty Blue is the perfect game. Some levels (particularly some of the "gimmick" levels) aren't that good. Off the top of my head I can name the coconuts level, where you have to eat 100 coconuts that periodically fall from some palm trees, and the oysters level, where you have to wait for three oysters to create pearls and eat them until you're big enough to eat the oysters themselves. But with most of the levels being more interesting, having more enemy variety, and just being less repetitive than the ones in Tasty Planet, I find it a more engaging game.

If I had to name another downside, it would be the relatively early end of the game. Whereas Tasty Planet went on to space and had the grey goo eventually eating the fabric of reality (not even kidding), Tasty Blue ends with the shark eating Earth from the inside, and then the Moon. It was still a satisfying experience regardless, but it makes me wonder how space levels would have looked like with Tasty Blue's "upgraded" gameplay.

I'm gonna be leaving comments on in case anyone wants to discuss or write a rebuttal (I know that many Tasty Planet fans thought that Tasty Blue was a letdown), but I'm gonna ask y'all to be civil about it. This is a silly little game that's not worth getting angry over.

This game marked the start of the decline of the Tasty Planet series; it isn't as bad as Tasty Plant Forever but is definitely a step down compared to its predecessors. Having been a longtime fan of the series, it was a disappointment at launch and continues to be a disappointment now, with my opinion not having changed coming back to it after 7 years.

The gameplay is similar to previous games, but this time takes place with a basic 2d side view perspective compared to the top-down perspective the previous games had. It also comes with some basic water physics and gravity that are cute enough and definitely fit the theme, but quickly get old as you play the game.

While I respect the design choice to make the game themed around the ocean as well as the change in gameplay and the fact that the game exists at all; the truth of the matter is that this choice heavily limited the developers when it came to designing the game and I feel like it kind of gimped more or less all aspects of the game. Credit to them for experimenting, but it definitely didn’t work out.

To start, there is much less variety across the board when it comes to both things to eat and level design as there is only really so much you can do with just aquatic themes and the constraint of both water and gravity. This is maybe most noticeable in the fact that there are no space levels in this game, and the overall scope is much smaller than before.

The majority of the levels also tend to be quite short, even more so than the previous games, with it being fairly common for levels to be under a minute long. There are also very few gimmick levels and the majority of the ones that do exist feel kind of half assed.

The problems revolving around medal difficulty and bonus levels also return. This time the medals are replaced with a 0–3 star rating system and fortunately the stars serve no purpose besides achievements this time, although the unforgiving timelimits for the stars are still just as bad as before. Unfortunately, the bonus levels are once again a playground for the developers cruel and sadistic experimentation. While there are some cool ideas in there; many of them are either basic and boring or frustratingly hard, either with complex mechanical skill requirements or unreasonable enemies.

I didn’t really like the direction they took with the art style of the game, going for a grimier and more realistic looking and in my opinion overall uglier looking art style. Unfortunately, this trend would continue in the next game in the series. 

Even the humor of the game is impacted by the aquatic design. It still has its signature goofy and absurdist humor but this time they have much less to work with and it all feels a little flat. The story is also a step down in quality, which was sad even though the story is a relatively small part of the game. The 3 different characters are neat enough but make no real difference and even collectively they aren’t as charming as the original grey goo.

The one thing that is still just as good is the choice of music, with 2 new aquatic themed tracks joining the soundtrack alongside the music of the previous games. Once again, they really fit the theme of the game and it is hard to imagine and improvement on it. 

My overall playtime for each playthrough was about 3.5 hours. The game is worse than both of its predecessors so unless you REALLY like the series, I would not recommend it, especially if it’s not on sale. Even if you do like the series, you will probably still be at least a little disappointed in it.

Now for the things i don't like, the dolphin levels are the majority of the game, probably 45%, and they almost all suck, they are the most boring, and the hardest, and i was having a good time with the goldfish levels, and then i got to the dolphin, and i was like "ahh so there's the tasty game experience im use to" but i will say, the nano shark levels and the goldfish levels are ok to good, i don't know why the nano shark sounds like an actual person when he eats, but that doesn't matter. I will say that the first nano shark level being like 8 minutes is wack, and i beat this game's story in one sitting too, so after forcing myself through the dolphin levels, just to get that nearly took me out, but i powered through because there is only 13 nano shark levels, so i finished it, and i liked the ending. Also we was back to a "tasty planet 1" like focus on the story, like there wasn't really any story to this game, so thats the 1 thing back for seconds does better then this game. I'll be honest, when this game ended i wanted to play it more, which is already better then the first 2, because i deleted them instantly, so i checked out the bonus levels on this game, and the only good thing i can say about them, is that the first pac-man inspired bonus level was good, the second one was horrible, and this game has literally made me hate manatees, because there is this one bonus level where you gotta eat grass before the 2 manatees do, and when i tell you i replayed it so many times, it started making me furious, so i figured this game wasn't worth my time anymore, so i deleted it. Hand down the best one out of the 3 so far, but im 85% sure that i shouldn't have wasted money on these games, like if they were free i'd recommend them more, but their not, so don't waste your money. if the first tasty planet is like a 3/10, and back for seconds is like a 5/10, id give this game like a 6/10. Almost gave it a half hearted thumbs up like i said, but the dolphin levels suck, and the bonus levels are rage inducing. I still have 1 "Tasty" game left to play, and i hope it alone will be worth the 30 bucks a spent to buy all 4 of them, but 3 games in and i seriously doubt it, but i hope im wrong, because im kinda ashamed that i thought these games were peak back in like 2017.
